newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-FIFA SET TO CONFIRM JAPAN AS HOSTS OF 2002 FINAL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FIFA SET TO CONFIRM JAPAN AS HOSTS OF 2002 FINAL.

text.p: FIFA, world soccer's governing body, are set to confirm the sport's worst-kept secret on Saturday when they formally annouce that Japan will host the World Cup final in 2002.
They will also confirm that South Korea, jointly hosting the tournament with their Asian neighbours, will stage the opening match of the finals in six years' time.

FIFA attempted to keep secret recommendations of the World Cup 2002 Study Group amid farcical scenes in Zurich a month ago when vice-president Lennart Johansson told 100 reporters that no information about the finals would be announced until this weekend.
But most of the details FIFA wanted to keep secret until endorsed by this weekend's executive committee meeting leaked out of Asia within hours.
A 33-point agenda will be set before the executive committee which is meeting, somewhat ironically, in Barcelona where Spain won the 1992 Olympic soccer tournament.

The irony will not be lost on the Spaniards because FIFA are considering a proposal to abolish the Olympic soccer tournament, which predates the World Cup by 30 years and was for three decades regarded as the unofficial world championship.

Instead FIFA are considering the introduction of an under-23 world championship -- which would serve to remove the anomalies of the Olympic tournament which has eligibility restrictions for some teams and not for others.

Despite the fact the Olympic tournament is no longer the dour, uninspiring competition it was when it was dominated by the old "amateur" teams of communist Eastern Europe, it still imposes restrictions on the more highly developed nations and also excludes teams from the home of soccer.

England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales are unable to compete as individual nations as they do in the World Cup because Britain sends one united team to the Olympic Games. But the four nations could compete in an under-23 competition which would be a huge boost to their younger professionals.

Among many other items, FIFA will be looking at ground safety, players' agents and a new initiative for the World Club Cup which has been played between the champions of Europe and South America 35 times since 1960. There is a possibility that the champion clubs of other confederations, including Asia, Africa and North America, could take part in an expanded tournament.
Two days before FIFA meets in Barcelona, UEFA's executive committee holds its own session in Tenerife.
UEFA officials, like FIFA's, are expected to annouce proposals on changes in the transfer system in the wake of last year's Bosman ruling, the future of national teams and of domestic leagues.

UEFA will also annouce the venues for this season's European Cup and Cup Winners' Cup finals and that the Czech Republic will represent Europe at next year's inaugural Confederations Cup for national teams in Saudi Arabia.
Germany, who should represent UEFA as European champions, have made it clear they will not compete in the tournament during their league season's mid-winter break.

UEFA will also hear a proposal from the German soccer association that the number of qualification matches for the 2000 European championship should be cut, leaving more dates free for lucrative friendlies.
